CausalChain: Chronic liver inflammation (HBV/HCV/cirrhosis) -> elevated inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL-6, TNF-α) -> upregulation of hepatic glycosyltransferases (e.g., FUT8, ST6GAL1) -> altered glycosylation of AFP -> increased conversion to AFP-L3 -> AFP-L3 engages oncogenic signaling & transcriptional networks -> aggressive tumor behavior (vascular invasion, poor differentiation) -> worsened prognosis in HCC
Hypothesis: In the context of chronic liver inflammation, elevated levels of inflammatory cytokines, particularly IL-6 and TNF-α, drive the upregulation of specific glycosyltransferases in hepatocytes. This upregulation results in aberrant glycosylation of AFP, favoring its conversion into the AFP-L3 isoform. Unlike traditional views that consider AFP-L3 solely as a biomarker, our hypothesis posits that AFP-L3 contributes to HCC pathogenesis by interacting with and modulating oncogenic signaling and transcription factor networks, thereby promoting aggressive tumor phenotypes such as increased vascular invasion and poor differentiation. We further hypothesize that inhibition or modulation of this cytokine–glycosyltransferase axis can both refine early diagnostic capabilities and provide a therapeutic avenue to mitigate HCC progression. Contemporary tools like CRISPR-based gene editing, single-cell transcriptomics, and high-resolution glycomics will be employed to validate these mechanistic insights.
Abstract: Chronic liver inflammation, hallmark of HBV/HCV infection and cirrhosis, is known to elevate inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 and TNF-α. We hypothesize that these cytokines upregulate specific hepatic glycosyltransferases (for example, FUT8 and ST6GAL1), which in turn modify the glycosylation pattern of alpha‐fetoprotein (AFP), increasing its conversion to the AFP-L3 isoform. Notably, beyond serving as a sensitive biomarker of early hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), AFP-L3 may actively engage oncogenic signaling pathways and transcription factor networks, thereby promoting tumor aggressiveness, including vascular invasion and poor differentiation. Leveraging contemporary technologies such as CRISPR gene editing, single-cell RNA sequencing, and advanced glycomics profiling, we propose to delineate the cytokine–glycosyltransferase axis in a mechanistic and clinically actionable framework. This integrative approach is intended to refine early detection strategies and facilitate targeted therapeutic interventions in HCC.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis proposed that inflammatory cytokines in chronic liver disease upregulate glycosyltransferases leading to an increased conversion of AFP to AFP-L3, which serves as both an early marker and a driver of tumor aggressiveness. The refined hypothesis maintains this essential causal chain while addressing reviewer concerns by specifying key cytokines (IL-6 and TNF-α) and glycosyltransferases (e.g., FUT8, ST6GAL1). It also links AFP-L3 to oncogenic signaling networks to account for the integration with broader cancer-associated gene expression profiles. Additionally, the new hypothesis leverages modern technological advances—such as CRISPR, single-cell RNA sequencing, and advanced glycomics—to bolster mechanistic validation and improve practical implementability for both diagnostic and therapeutic applications.
